prompt:
Surprise me — build a small playable game (specifically: dave (Dangerous Dave-style platformer)) in vanilla HTML/CSS/JS that I can preview right now. Aesthetic: a tropical jungle palette (deep green, papaya, ivory). Make it visually impressive, modern, and polished. The specific pick and the aesthetic are FIXED for your decisions — don't substitute a different game / widget / piece if you think it's safer, and don't drift to a different palette on your own initiative mid-build. How you design and structure the build is fully up to you. If I ask for a different category, aesthetic, theme, or palette in a follow-up, my follow-up wins. Avoid the word "aurora" anywhere in the page or filenames — pick fresh names.

This one has to run smoothly on low-end student laptops and still look great, so:
- World-building first: a side-scrolling jungle-temple level a few screens wide with parallax background layers, animated water, torches and vines, collectible gems and a key, a few patrolling enemies, hazards, and an exit door that needs the key. Pixel-art style, with every sprite and tile drawn in code — no external assets, fonts or libraries.
- Render on a small fixed internal canvas (about 320x180) scaled up with CSS image-rendering: pixelated. 2D canvas only — no WebGL or 3D. Pre-render tiles and sprites to offscreen canvases once. No shadowBlur, no getImageData or per-pixel work, no large particle counts. Step the game with delta time, cap the step, and pause when the tab is hidden.
- Attract mode: until the player presses a key or taps, the game plays itself (a simple scripted player runs the level on a loop) so the preview is alive with nobody touching it. Show a small 'Press any key to play' prompt; any input hands control to the player.
- Controls: arrow keys / WASD and Space to jump, plus on-screen touch buttons for trackpad and touch users. HUD with gems, key and lives. Win and game-over screens with restart.
- Sound off by default (tiny WebAudio bleeps behind a mute toggle are fine).
- When you test with execJsInLivePreview keep every check short and cheap: read state, no long synchronous loops, no simulating long stretches of gameplay in one call, no canvas readbacks, no synthetic input storms. A few quick checks and screenshots are enough.

CRITICAL: Always create a BRAND NEW HTML file for this build. Do NOT Read, Edit, or Write into any file that already existed before this task started — whatever file the user has open is irrelevant, do not touch it. Call getEditorState ONCE up front if you need to learn the project root path (so your Write call uses a correct absolute path), but ignore the active file it reports — that's not your target. Pick a fresh filename that matches the pick (e.g. `<pick-name>.html`) and use the Write tool to create it from scratch in the project root. After that file is created, you SHOULD use Edit on it freely for the incremental build steps below — the rule is only about not touching pre-existing files.

Build it INCREMENTALLY so I see it come together like a person is hand-building it — never write the whole thing in one Write call:
1. Start by building a task list with TaskCreate (one call per step: scaffold, sections/features, styling, animations, polish). Use TaskUpdate to mark each step in_progress when you start it and completed when you finish, so progress is always visible.
2. Write a minimal scaffold HTML file first (a NEW file via the Write tool — not an Edit of any existing file) — basic structure and placeholder content, just enough that something appears in the live preview within a few seconds.
3. Enhance progressively in coherent chunks — one section, one feature, or one cohesive style/animation block at a time. Each Edit should produce a visible change in the preview but stay focused enough to render quickly. Don't write the whole page in one giant rewrite, and don't fragment into atomic single-property edits — aim for meaningful steps the user can watch land.
4. Take screenshots only at logical milestones (e.g. after the scaffold lands, after a major section is complete, at the end) — not after every small edit.
5. At the end, test and inspect the page using execJsInLivePreview — verify there are no console errors and that the controls respond. Keep it to a few cheap checks. Fix anything broken before declaring done.

Use a cohesive design, smooth animations, and a fully responsive layout. Save to a single NEW HTML file (created via Write, not by editing an existing file). Build it in the user's locale (en-US).

data.text:
built the game as a new single file, `dave-jungle-temple.html`, and it is open in your live preview, playing itself in demo mode until you press a key or tap. I did not edit any existing file in the project.

I tested it two ways:
- **Offline simulation:** I ran the demo player through the level outside the preview at 30, 45, 60 and 144 fps. It finished every loop in about 16 seconds with zero deaths and always picked up the key before reaching the door.
- **Live preview:** A key press hands control to you, and the player moves and collects gems. The win and game-over screens appear and restart correctly, the layout holds at phone width, and there were no console errors.

The real sound effects, tapping the on-screen buttons, and an actual death were not exercised in the preview.

## The level
- **World:** A jungle-temple level about 4.8 screens wide, drawn entirely in code in deep green, papaya and ivory. It has layered parallax backgrounds, torches, swaying vines, animated water and fireflies.
- **Collectibles and exit:** 32 gems, including bonus ones on high platforms inside the temple. The key sits on a stone pedestal in the temple, and the exit door at the far end stays locked until you have it.
- **Hazards:** Spikes and water kill you.
- **Enemies:** Two snakes and two bats patrol, and you can stomp them.
- **Lives:** You have three lives, with checkpoints along the way.

## Controls
- **Keyboard:** Arrow keys or WASD move, and Space jumps.
- **Touch:** The on-screen ◀ ▶ and Jump buttons work for touch and trackpad.
- **Restart:** Enter or R restarts from the end screens.
- **Sound:** Off by default. M or the button in the header toggles it, and it stays silent during the demo even when turned on.

## Performance
The canvas is a fixed 320×180, scaled up with pixelated rendering. The static level, tiles and sprites are drawn once at load, and particles are capped at 48. The game loop caps its time step and stops while the tab is hidden.
